newsitem.title: PERU: Peru government closes ranks around security aide.
newsitem.headline: Peru government closes ranks around security aide.

text.p: The Peruvian government closed ranks on Friday around its shadowy security adviser, Vladimiro Montesinos, who has been under pressure since a captured drug lord accused him of protecting traffickers.

In an overnight congressional hearing that lasted nearly 12 hours, the defence, interior and prime ministers strenuously defended Montesinos and praised him as a key part of Peru's wars on communist guerrillas and drug traffickers.

In response to opposition legislators, Prime Minister Alberto Pandolfi implicity denied the charge of involvement in the drug trade, saying Montesinos played "a fundamental role in the drawing up of very important laws against this social scourge."
He said Montesinos also drew up "a series of laws which paved the way for the war against subversion which culminated in the capture of (Shining Path guerrilla leader) Abimael Guzman."

Montesinos, a lawyer and legal adviser to the National Intelligence Service (SIN), was accused by confessed drug trafficker Demetrio Chavez last month of accepting $50,000 per month in 1991 to protect activities in Peru's drug heartland, the Upper Huallaga Valley.

Defence Minister Juan Castillo Meza acknowledged that Montesinos had been tried for treason by a military court in 1983 but said he had been found innocent. Castillo attacked claims that Montesinos had been dismissed from the army as "false and calumnious."
Opposition legislators, a former army major and local media have claimed that Montesinos was kicked out of the army for selling U.S. CIA agents a list of Peruvian arms purchases in Russia.
Castillo also branded as "fantasy" claims that Montesinos aided the military of Ecuador, which Peru fought in a brief border war last year.

Interior Minister Juan Briones Davila denied that Montesinos had been behind two of Peru's most notorious human rights abuses -- the 1992 execution by an army death squad of nine students and a professor at La Cantuta University and the 1991 military massacre of 15 partygoers in a Lima house.

Opposition legislators said the ministers were engaging in a coverup and had given no evidence to support their defence of Montesinos, who is seldom seen in public but is widely regarded as President Alberto Fujimori's right-hand man.
"The ministers have only told us half-truths," opposition legislator Henry Pease said during the debate.

Chavez's accusation against Montesinos in August unleashed a tide of criticism of the security adviser. But Montesinos has so far remained silent, ignoring a recommendation from Fujimori that he defend himself publicly.
Chavez recently retracted his accusation, saying he had been "confused." But his change of mind brought claims in the media that intelligence officers had influenced him in prison.

Opinion polls show more than 90 percent of Peruvians are unconvinced by the government's defence of Montesinos and want a full investigation of his critics' claims and a detailed explanation of his work in the government.
